title: The harp (1 Samuel 16:14–23)
hook: young David plays, and the troubled king is refreshed

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eliab, passed over, and your line was god looks on the heart.

Yesterday ended with the Spirit of the LORD coming upon David. The very next verse: "But the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD troubled him." One young man filled. One king emptied, and tormented. Nothing says Saul's servants know about the oil in Bethlehem. What they can see is that their king is not well. Find a man who can play the harp, they say, and when the trouble comes on you, he'll play with his hand, "and thou shalt be well."

Start with the hard phrase: an evil spirit from the LORD. Readers have wrestled with it. Some understand it as a real spiritual being that God permits to trouble Saul. Others read it as the text's way of saying that Saul's own darkness, his fear and his rage, became a kind of judgment. Some modern readers hear something like deep anguish or depression, though the text doesn't use our words, and gives no diagnosis. Whatever it is, it comes in waves, and it hurts. Then one servant names a name: "I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, that is cunning in playing." Brave, he adds, a man of war, prudent, comely, and the LORD is with him. So Saul sends to Jesse: "Send me David thy son, which is with the sheep." The anointed boy walks into the court of the king he'll replace, with a donkey laden with bread, a bottle of wine and a young goat from his father. The text says Saul loves him greatly and makes him his armor bearer. Nothing in the text says Saul knows who he's hired. The Hebrew word for the instrument is kinnor, a stringed instrument; the King James says harp, and some modern translations say lyre. Then the chapter's last verse: "when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him." Refreshed. No speech, no fix for what was wrong. Just a boy, a few strings, and a tormented man able to breathe again, for now.
screen: `CUNNING IN PLAYING, AND THE LORD WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: If you can, put on one quiet piece of music, play something yourself, or hum; if you can't, listen to the quietest sounds around you as if they were music. If you pray, the Psalms are there to borrow. Music can help, but when the trouble is heavy it isn't the only help, and reaching for a person is part of the cure too.
The harp. David's kinnor in Saul's court. When the trouble came on the king, David played with his hand, and Saul was refreshed, and was well.
Your line: music can heal. Saul was refreshed, and was well, for a time. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians sing and play music as part of worship, and some point to David playing for Saul when they talk about music as comfort for the troubled.

chat.says: Did David's music actually help King Saul?
options: The text says so: Saul was refreshed and well, and the evil spirit left him.
No, Saul couldn't stand it and sent David back to his sheep that day.
Yes, it cured him for good, and the trouble never came back again.

notes: Audit: all KJV quotations checked against the 1769 text; no changes needed.

Three readings of 'an evil spirit from the LORD' (a spiritual being God permits; Saul's own darkness as judgment; something like anguish or depression) are offered without ranking. Mental-health wording is careful not to diagnose and the practice notes music is not the only help.
Editor: cut the unsourced description of the kinnor as small and held in the arms (teach, myth, trapdoor); the myth item about a concert harp replaced with one from 16:20 (the gifts Jesse sent).

Editor 2: hook no longer opens 'Two...' the day before day 716's 'Two armies'; 'and the LORD is with him' unquoted (not in sources); what the servants and Saul knew softened to what the text says; myth 1 (Saul did not know of the anointing, which the text never states) replaced with 16:21.
Possible tension with 1 Samuel 17:55–58, where Saul asks whose son David is, is left for tomorrow and later lessons.
